en: A temporary alternative path around a closed or blocked road.
Small loose stones on the road surface that can reduce tyre grip.
A large goods truck used to carry heavy loads (UK term for a truck).
A lower gear ratio that gives more engine control at slower speeds, often used on hills.
A UK document showing a vehicle has passed its annual roadworthiness test.
The date when the current MOT certificate runs out and a new test is needed.
The UK annual check that a vehicle is safe and roadworthy.
The annual UK roadworthiness test required for most vehicles over a certain age.
UK annual roadworthiness tests (MOT) checking safety and emissions.
Full high-beam headlights that light farther ahead but can dazzle other drivers.
High-beam headlights that light farther ahead but can dazzle other road users.
An order you must follow, not just advice.
Rules you are legally required to obey.
The official owner’s manual from the car maker explaining controls and systems.
A UK personal tax and benefits reference number, not a driving document.
A restriction meaning goods must not be loaded or unloaded there at the times shown.
You must not leave the vehicle parked, but brief stopping to drop off may be allowed.
A ban on stopping your vehicle at all, even briefly (stricter than no parking).
A UK restriction meaning you must not wait or park there at the times shown.
Rubber or metal rings that stop oil leaking from the engine.
The headlights of vehicles coming toward you from the opposite direction.
A road where traffic is allowed to travel in only one direction.
Run the engine at very high revs, which wastes fuel and can cause wear.
To pass another vehicle by moving past it and going ahead.
Vehicles that are passing you on the road.
Passing a slower vehicle ahead by moving into another lane or the other side of the road.
Optional plates some newly qualified drivers display to show they have just passed their test.
Emergency medical staff who treat patients at the scene and in ambulances.
Low-intensity lights used to show a parked or stationary vehicle’s position.
Small electric vehicles used by people with limited mobility.
A main A-road network in the UK, usually signed with green direction signs.
Flags or lights that mark an overhanging load so other road users can see it.
Drive level with another vehicle, side by side.
Bright red lights at the back of a vehicle used only in thick fog to help others see you.
The person named on the vehicle’s registration document as responsible for it (not always the owner).
Air above an area where flying is limited or controlled for safety.
Make the engine run faster while the vehicle is not moving forward much.
Holding the clutch partly down while driving, which can wear it and reduce control.
A vehicle that spreads salt or grit on roads to reduce ice in cold weather.
A warning that the carriageway becomes narrower ahead.
A slow vehicle that cleans the road surface; give it space when passing.
Vehicle Excise Duty — the UK government charge for using a vehicle on public roads.
Construction or repairs on the road that may change lanes or reduce speed.
Road repairs or construction that may change layout, lanes, or speed limits.
A declaration that a vehicle is kept off public roads and is not taxed for road use.
A path that pedestrians and cyclists may both use.
Low-power front and rear position lights; not bright enough alone for driving at speed.
A warning that the road surface may be slippery.
A road that is wet, icy, or otherwise hard for tyres to grip.
A road surface with poor grip, so vehicles can skid more easily.
A vehicle that clears snow from the road, often with a blade at the front.
A camera that records vehicles breaking the speed limit.
Cameras that detect vehicles exceeding the speed limit.
Raised sections across the road designed to slow traffic down.
A device that reduces unwanted swinging or swaying of a trailer while towing.
The springs and related parts that connect the wheels to the car body and absorb bumps.
A junction where one road meets another and ends, forming a ‘T’ shape.
A short-term alternative route when the normal road cannot be used.
Short-term alternative routes when the normal road is closed or blocked.
One or more lanes closed for a limited time, often during road works.
Short-term construction or repairs that change normal road conditions.
Portable signals used for a limited time, often at road works.
Insurance that covers injury/damage to others, plus fire damage and theft of your vehicle.
A belt that keeps engine valves and pistons moving in the correct timing.
Places of interest for visitors, such as landmarks or museums.
Road features designed to slow vehicles down, such as humps or narrowings.
The system that transfers engine power to the wheels, including the gearbox.
Traffic moving in both directions on the same road.
How well the tyres hold onto the road surface without sliding.
Tyres with too little air; can raise fuel use and affect braking.
Turning the vehicle all the way round to go back the way you came.
